newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top german economist says Amsterdam pact a threat.
newsitem.headline: Top german economist says Amsterdam pact a threat.

text.p: The stability and growth pact agreed by European leaders last week in Amsterdam constitutes a danger to the independence of the future European Central Bank (ECB) and may have disastrous consequences for Europe's economy, a leading German economist said on Sunday.

"I consider this chapter a threat to the independence of the (European) central bank," Horst Siebert, a member of the government's "five wise men" economic advisory council, said in an interview with the Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
He was referring to the resolution on employment and growth added to the original 'stability pact' before it was finally agreed at the EU summit in Amsterdam.
The stability pact is designed to ensure budgetary discipline in Europe after the introduction of the euro single currency in 1999.

"I am afraid, that with the employment chapter included, the coordinated monetary policy system will be pushed back -- pushed away from a policy of a stable euro and towards a policy aiming at job creation," Siebert said.
"If it were to come to such a paradigmatic change, this could have devastating consequences."

Asked if he meant the future euro single currency could be misused in order to stimulate Europe's economy, Siebert, who is also president of the IfW economic institute in Kiel, told the newspaper: "After Amsterdam, that danger is there."
The IfW is one of Germany's six leading institutes.
Siebert added that unemployment could not in any case be solved by agreements signed at summits, since the cause of joblessness was different in every country.

In France, youth unemployment had been aggravated by a minimum wage policy, while Germany's labour markets were suffering above all under the burden of high wage levels and structual problems, he said.
Last week, the Munich-based Ifo economic research institute said unemployment levels in Gernany would begin to subside once annual economic growth reached rates of more than 2.3 percent.
But Siebert said that with unemployment at such critical levels, growth rates were of limited consequence. "Growth alone cannot eliminate Germany's jobs crisis."

He said longer-term studies showed labour markets were barely affected at growth rates of two percent. Beyond there, around 100,000 jobs were created for every percentage point of additional growth, he said.

But he added: "With 4.3 million people out of work, that doesn't help us much....Firstly, in Germany we are still a long way away from sustained growth of three percent or more, and secondly, what good are 100,000 new jobs to us?"
While he noted the country's relatively healthy export sector, Siebert warned against neglecting further efforts to ensure Germany's fitness for international competition.

"There is no way to avoid greater wage differentials. The global economy is on the brink of radical change. Overnight, fresh labour forces will come onto the market, producing at a fraction of German wage costs," Siebert said.
Siebert cited Asia and eastern Europe as examples of recent additions to global labour markets, saying available worldwide labour had inceased by a quarter in the last few years.
"That wage levels have suffered as a result is of course clear," he said.

Siebert said far-reaching reform of Germany's social welfare system was needed, suggesting that employers themselves should bear the costs of short-term sickness, leaving the welfare system to handle longer-term cases of unemployment or inability to work.
